quests.sentenceWithBlank: Her grandmother was diagnosed with ___ diabetes last year.
quests.completedSentence: Her grandmother was diagnosed with diabetes last year.
quests.ruleExplanation: Serious illness names like diabetes, cancer, and pneumonia take no article in standard English.
quests.nativeTip: Serious illness names usually stand alone without an article.
quests.example: Her grandmother was diagnosed with diabetes last year.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: I think I'm coming down with ___ cold.
quests.completedSentence: I think I'm coming down with a cold.
quests.grammarRule: Indefinite article before a consonant sound
quests.ruleExplanation: Unlike diabetes or cancer, everyday minor ailments like 'a cold', 'a headache', and 'a fever' take the indefinite article — 'cold' begins with a consonant sound.
quests.nativeTip: This minor ailment behaves differently from the more serious illness names.
quests.visualAnchor: 🔤 a: Indefinite article before a consonant sound
quests.example: I think I'm coming down with a cold.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: He's been undergoing treatment for ___ cancer for the past six months.
quests.completedSentence: He's been undergoing treatment for cancer for the past six months.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Cancer', like other serious illness names, takes no article in standard English.
quests.nativeTip: This follows the same pattern as diabetes — a serious illness name standing alone.
quests.example: He's been undergoing treatment for cancer for the past six months.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: She speaks fluent ___ Spanish, so she'll be able to help us during the trip.
quests.completedSentence: She speaks fluent Spanish, so she'll be able to help us during the trip.
quests.ruleExplanation: Language names like Spanish, French, and Mandarin take no article when used this way.
quests.nativeTip: Language names usually stand alone without an article.
quests.example: She speaks fluent Spanish, so she'll be able to help us during the trip.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: ___ Spanish language has many regional variations across Latin America.
quests.completedSentence: the Spanish language has many regional variations across Latin America.
quests.ruleExplanation: When the word 'language' is explicitly included after the name, the phrase behaves like an ordinary noun phrase and takes 'the' — 'the Spanish language'.
quests.nativeTip: This time, the word 'language' itself is stated explicitly.
quests.example: the Spanish language has many regional variations across Latin America.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: He's been studying ___ Mandarin for almost two years now.
quests.completedSentence: He's been studying Mandarin for almost two years now.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Mandarin', like other language names, takes no article on its own.
quests.nativeTip: This follows the same pattern as Spanish — a language name standing alone.
quests.example: He's been studying Mandarin for almost two years now.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: We always spend ___ Christmas with my grandparents in the countryside.
quests.completedSentence: We always spend Christmas with my grandparents in the countryside.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Christmas', like other named holidays, takes no article in everyday statements.
quests.nativeTip: Named holidays usually stand alone without an article.
quests.example: We always spend Christmas with my grandparents in the countryside.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: We had ___ wonderful Christmas last year, despite the terrible weather.
quests.completedSentence: We had a wonderful Christmas last year, despite the terrible weather.
quests.ruleExplanation: When Christmas is described as a specific, memorable occasion with an adjective like 'wonderful', it behaves like other countable nouns and takes 'a' — the same pattern seen earlier with 'a lovely dinner'.
quests.nativeTip: When a holiday is described as one particular, memorable occasion, it behaves differently.
quests.example: We had a wonderful Christmas last year, despite the terrible weather.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: ___ Thanksgiving always brings our whole family together.
quests.completedSentence: Thanksgiving always brings our whole family together.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Thanksgiving', like other named holidays, takes no article.
quests.nativeTip: This follows the same pattern as Christmas — a named holiday standing alone.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The kids spent the whole afternoon watching ___ television.
quests.completedSentence: The kids spent the whole afternoon watching television.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Television' in the sense of the activity or medium takes no article — we say 'watch television', not 'watch a television'.
quests.nativeTip: This describes the general activity or medium, not one physical object.
quests.visualAnchor: 🚫 (no article): Fixed expression with zero article
quests.example: The kids spent the whole afternoon watching television.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: We always listen to ___ radio during our morning commute.
quests.completedSentence: We always listen to the radio during our morning commute.
quests.ruleExplanation: Interestingly, 'the radio' keeps 'the' even when talking about the medium in general, unlike 'television' — this is simply an established exception to memorize.
quests.nativeTip: Unlike television, this medium keeps its article even in the general sense.
quests.example: We always listen to the radio during our morning commute.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Could you turn off ___ television? It's getting late.
quests.completedSentence: Could you turn off the television? It's getting late.
quests.ruleExplanation: Here 'television' refers to the specific physical device in the room, so it takes 'the', a different meaning from the general activity in the first question.
quests.nativeTip: This time, it's the specific physical object in the room.
quests.example: Could you turn off the television? It's getting late.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Please submit your complaint in ___ writing rather than over the phone.
